2322447.title: NHRC, India organises a National Conference on the theme ‘Water as the Elixir of Life: Advancing Human Dignity through the Right to Water’ on its 33rd Foundation Day in New Delhi
2322447.body_html:
National Human Rights Commission
NHRC, India organises a National Conference on the theme ‘Water as the Elixir of Life: Advancing Human Dignity through the Right to Water’ on its 33rd Foundation Day in New Delhi
Emphasising action must begin immediately, NHRC Chairperson, Justice V. Ramasubramanian says, the present generation owes a responsibility to preserve natural resources for future generations
The Conference deliberates on various human rights dimensions of water security, conservation and sustainable management
Posted On: 12 OCT 2026 7:12PM by PIB Delhi

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), India organised a National Conference on the theme ‘Water as the Elixir of Life: Advancing Human Dignity through the Right to Water’ at Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi today, as part of the celebrations marking its 33rd Foundation Day. The Conference brought together representatives of government institutions, development organisations and other stakeholders to deliberate on the human rights dimensions of access to safe drinking water, sustainable management of water resources, rejuvenation of water bodies, community participation and the need to strengthen institutional mechanisms for ensuring water security.

Addressing the first session on ‘Water conservation, sustainability and community participation’ Shri Brijendra Swaroop, Executive Director (Projects), National Mission for Clean Ganga, Ministry of Jal Shakti emphasised that non-discriminatory access to adequate, safe and affordable water is fundamental to human dignity. Outlining the Namami Gange Programme, he highlighted its Integrated River Basin Management approach and the objectives of ensuring Nirmal Dhara (unpolluted flow), Aviral Dhara (continuous flow) and protection of the Ganga’s geological and ecological integrity. The programme comprises 527 projects with a sanctioned cost of approximately Rs 43,326 crore, covering pollution abatement, ecological restoration, biodiversity conservation, community participation, research and livelihood enhancement.

He stressed the need for comprehensive wastewater management, maintenance of ecological flows, protection of floodplains, wetland restoration and biodiversity conservation. Referring to improvements in water quality in several stretches of the Ganga, he observed that the success of rejuvenation efforts should be assessed through environmental outcomes, including water quality, biodiversity and ecosystem functioning, rather than expenditure or the number of completed projects alone. He called for scientific mapping of water bodies, catchment-based planning, institutional convergence and community participation, emphasising that conservation must precede restoration.

Shri Yugal Kishore Joshi, Programme Director, NITI Aayog highlighted India’s water-security challenges, noting that the country has approximately 4% of the world’s freshwater resources but nearly 18% of its population. Per capita water availability has declined to approximately 1,300–1,400 cubic metres annually, below the water-stress threshold of 1,700 cubic metres. He emphasised integrating traditional water-harvesting practices with modern scientific methods, strengthening Gram Panchayats, preparing water budgets and addressing encroachment.

Citing a community-led initiative covering approximately 800 villages, in which water-body rejuvenation had been completed in 731 villages at an approximate cost of Rs. 3 lakh per water body, he highlighted the importance of community labour and productive use of excavated silt. He called for stronger local institutions, improved monitoring and wider replication of successful conservation initiatives.

Ms.Anjali Makhija, CEO and Trustee, S M Sehgal Foundation highlighted the importance of collaboration among communities, government, development organisations, academia and other stakeholders in addressing water and agricultural challenges. She outlined the Foundation’s work on groundwater recharge, supplementary surface-water storage, rainwater harvesting in schools, water quality and climate-smart, water-efficient agriculture, including drip and sprinkler irrigation and laser land levelling.

She emphasised the role of women’s groups and village development committees in identifying priorities, contributing resources and maintaining water structures. Stressing the need to work in coordination with local and district administrations, she advocated combining traditional knowledge with scientific expertise through GIS mapping, soil-moisture and water-quality monitoring as well as third-party assessments. She also called for affordable and accessible technology, greater philanthropic and CSR investment in water and agriculture, besides the development of a scientifically designed water-credit system.

Dr. Rajendra Singh, Chairperson, Tarun Bharat Sanghemphasised that water has its own rights and that rivers must remain nirmal (pure) and aviral (flowing uninterruptedly), with their ecological integrity protected alongside the human right to water. Reflecting on India’s natural wealth and its decline, he highlighted his experience of restoring 23 rivers through community participation, traditional water-conservation practices and ecological restoration.

He stressed that the right to water must go hand in hand with the responsibility to protect rivers and their natural ecosystems. Emphasising that knowledge and advocacy must translate into meaningful environmental action, he called for drawing upon traditional wisdom to conserve natural resources, restore rivers and preserve ecological balance for future generations.

Addressing the second session on ‘Strengthening drinking-water services and local governance’ Shri Ashok K. K. Meena, Secretary, Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation, Ministry of Jal Shakti emphasised that safe drinking water is integral to human dignity, public health and the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution.

Referring to the Jal Jeevan Mission, launched in 2019, he stated that approximately 82% of the planned water-connection infrastructure had been created. He noted that approximately 25% of blocks were in critical, semi-critical or over-exploited groundwater categories. Surface water-dependent schemes had increased from 15% to 48%, while groundwater-dependent schemes had declined from 85% to 52%.

He called for village-level water budgeting, source sustainability, digital monitoring and stronger Gram Panchayats and Village Water and Sanitation Committees. Highlighting water-quality surveillance, he noted that approximately 2.4 million women had been trained to use field-testing kits and upload data for remedial action. He stressed interdepartmental convergence and referred to completing infrastructure under Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 by December 2028, ensuring safe, reliable and sustainable drinking-water services.

Shri Uma Shankar Pandey, noted social worker, farmer and groundwater conservationist emphasised the vital importance of water conservation through collective stakeholder efforts. He highlighted concerns regarding the commercialisation and wastage of water and stressed that ensuring access to safe drinking water is a shared responsibility of the Government and the community. He underscored the need for water literacy, community participation and revival of traditional water-management practices. Using the example of a little bird attempting to extinguish a forest fire, he highlighted the significance of individual contributions. Emphasising the importance of awareness creation, he asserted that building a New Bharat must begin with individual responsibility. He reiterated his slogan, “Khetmein med, med par ped”, advocating tree plantation on agricultural field bundsas a sustainable water-conservation practice.

Shri Anand Shekhar, CEO, Water Aid India appreciated the NHRC, India’s focus on water as a fundamental human right. He stressed that every household tap must be supported by a sustainable water source to ensure reliable access. Recalling that sanitation coverage in India was below 20% in 2014, he highlighted the progress achieved in eliminating open defecation and extending sustainable sanitation services to all rural households within five years through political leadership, public investment and community participation.

He noted that approximately 86% of households now have access to drinking-water services through functional household tap connections. He also highlighted the opportunity presented by the allocation of approximately Rs. 8 lakh crore placed at the disposal of Gram Panchayats, of which 50% earmarked for water and sanitation, enabling nearly 2.5 lakh Gram Panchayats to strengthen service delivery. Emphasising source sustainability under the Jal Jeevan Mission, he called for political and administrative ownership, adequate public financing, inter-ministerial coordination, multi-stakeholder partnerships and greater community mobilisation. He underlined that the objective must go beyond coverage to ensure “water for everyone and for always” through reliable, quality and sustainable drinking-water services.

In the concluding session, Justice V. Ramasubramanian, Chairperson, NHRC expressed gratitude to the participants and highlighted the significance of the PanchBhoota, the five elements of nature, in sustaining life and maintaining ecological balance. Reflecting on the properties of water, he appreciated the collaborative approach to conservation advocated by the panellists and stressed collective efforts and stakeholder participation. He highlighted the contradiction between reverence and action, observing that society often fails to protect what it reveres, citing women and water as examples. He called for responsible behaviour and sustained conservation efforts to bridge this gap.

The Chairperson emphasised that conservation efforts must begin immediately, noting that the present generation has benefited from the efforts and sacrifices of its ancestors and has a responsibility to preserve natural resources for future generations. He underscored the cumulative impact of individual and collective efforts, stressing that conservation initiatives require a long-term vision, even when results take decades to emerge. He called for timely, sustained and collaborative action to safeguard water resources for present and future generations.

Shri Piyush Goyal, Secretary General, NHRC summarised the deliberations of the two thematic sessions. He emphasised the urgency of addressing climate change and severe groundwater depletion through decentralised, community-led governance involving Gram Panchayats, village-level water and sanitation committees, women’s groups and civil society. He stressed that, although significant ground-level work remained, close coordination among government agencies, civil society and local communities would help ensure a positive and sustainable way forward.

Shri Samir Kumar, Joint Secretary, NHRC, India delivered the vote of thanks expressing gratitude to the Chief Guest, the Chief Justice of India, for accepting the invitation and sharing his insights.

He also thanked the NHRC Chairperson and Members for their guidance and leadership and representatives of Ministries, government departments, civil society organisations and other participants for their valuable contributions. He acknowledged the efforts of all those involved in organising the conference and reiterated the collective commitment to the promotion and protection of human rights.

*****

2322445.title: Citizen Centric Pan-India Rail Jan Samvaad to Be Held at All Stations on 22.10.2026
2322445.body_html:
Ministry of Railways
Citizen Centric Pan-India Rail Jan Samvaad to Be Held at All Stations on 22.10.2026
Secretary, Railway Board Reviews Progress of Special Campaign 6 Across Indian Railways
Ongoing Special Campaign Focuses on Measurable Outcomes and Waste to Wonder Initiatives
Target to Clean 1 Lakh Sites, Clear 7 Lakh Sq. Ft. of Space and Generate ₹600 Crore from Scrap and E-Waste Disposal by Month End
Posted On: 12 OCT 2026 7:06PM by PIB Delhi

A high-level review meeting was held through video conferencing on 08.10.2026 at Railway Board under the chairmanship of Secretary, Railway Board to reinforce and review the progress of Special Campaign for Disposal of Pending Matters 6 (SCDPM-6) on the Zonal Railways/Units. AGMs of Zonal Railways, DRMs and ADRMs of Divisions, CPROs of Zonal Railways, GMs of Production Units, CMDs/MDs of Railway PSUs, DGs of Training Institutes, Concerned officers of Railway Board and Nodal Officers of SCDPM 6 in field units participated in the meeting.

The meeting reviewed progress against campaign targets, with focus on measurable outcomes and timely disposal of pending matters. Indian Railways has set targets of 1,00,000 cleanliness sites, freeing of 7,00,000 sq. ft. of space and generation of ₹600 crore through scrap disposal.

In line with this year's focus, special emphasis is placed on "Effective Collection, Segregation, and Disposal of E-Waste" as per E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, scrap disposal under GFR. Good practices, including Waste to Wonder, are also being identified for wider adoption.

The citizen-centric component of the campaign includes Rail Jan Samvaad, with Rail Jan Yuva Samvaad providing a dedicated platform for youth participation. Pan-India Rail Jan Samvaad is scheduled at all stations on 22.10.2026.

Some of the key initiatives of Special Campaign 6 adopted across Indian Railways are highlighted below:

  • Cleanliness Drive at Hazrat Nizamuddin Station, Delhi.

2322443.title: Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan Felicitates Top-Performing Districts at PM Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana’s National Conference
2322443.body_html:
Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare
Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan Felicitates Top-Performing Districts at PM Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana’s National Conference
Convergence of Schemes Transforms Ground Realities: Shri Chouhan Calls for Coordinated Action to Boost Farm Incomes
From Water Conservation to Natural Farming: District-Level Innovations Offer a Roadmap for Agricultural Growth
Shri Chouhan Calls for Higher Farm Credit in Eastern India, Pulses Cultivation in Rice Fallow Areas
No Goal Is Impossible with Determination: Shri Chouhan Urges Collectors to Accelerate Agricultural Development
District-Led Planning and Inter-Ministerial Coordination Key to Agricultural Growth: Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan
Posted On: 12 OCT 2026 7:05PM by PIB Delhi

When policies are shaped by ground realities and all government departments work together in one direction, no district can be left behind in the race for development. This is the hallmark of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s model of good governance, Union Minister for Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare and Rural Development Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan said on Monday. He was addressing the national conference on the Prime Minister Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana at the Bharat Ratna C. Subramaniam Auditorium in the Pusa campus, New Delhi. Addressing district collectors, scientists and senior policymakers from more than 50 districts across the country, Shri Chouhan extended his greetings on the auspicious occasion of Navratri and felicitated districts that had demonstrated outstanding performance. He urged officials to devote their full energy to realising Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s vision of a developed and prosperous India.

Districts at the Centre of Agricultural Planning

Emphasising the importance of localised planning, Chouhan said the framework for the PM Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana had been prepared by district collectors based on actual ground conditions rather than being drawn up in offices in Delhi. He stressed the need for regular monthly reviews, asking collectors to assess progress on their district agricultural action plans every month along with their teams. Where progress is slow, coordinated efforts across departments should be intensified to accelerate implementation. Highlighting the importance of inter-ministerial convergence, Shri Chouhan said farmers’ incomes could be increased manifold by bringing together the efforts of different ministries and institutions. These include the Ministry of Jal Shakti for water management; the Ministry of Food Processing Industries for processing and value addition; the Ministry of Cooperation and Farmer Producer Organisations for strengthening collective efforts; and the sectors of animal husbandry, dairy, fisheries, MSMEs and skill development. He also emphasised the need to strengthen the direct connection between agricultural research and farmers. Research conducted by nearly 16,000 scientists associated with the Indian Council of Agricultural Research, along with the work of Krishi Vigyan Kendras, the Agricultural Technology Management Agency and agricultural universities, should reach farmers’ fields directly.

Focus on Low Productivity, Rice Fallow Areas and Credit Flow

Shri Chouhan said PMDDKY prioritises 100 districts that have lagged in agricultural productivity, have low cropping intensity or face inadequate institutional credit flow. He directed officials to promote pulses and oilseeds in rice fallow areas, where fields remain uncultivated after paddy harvesting, through a mission-mode approach. Expanding cultivation in these areas would help improve land utilisation and agricultural output. He also called for wider coverage of the Kisan Credit Card scheme and a faster flow of institutional credit, particularly in eastern India and underdeveloped districts. Farmers need access to capital to adopt advanced agricultural technologies and use better seeds and fertilisers, he said.

Chouhan Calls on Officials to Work with Determination

Motivating officials to pursue ambitious development goals, Shri Chouhan quoted the well-known lines: “Who says a hole cannot be made in the sky? Just throw a stone with conviction, my friends…” Encouraging district collectors to approach their responsibilities with determination, he shared the following lines:

If you wish, you can break mountains and hills;

If you wish, you can change the course of rivers;

If you wish, you can extract nectar from the soil;

If you wish, you can connect the earth with the sky!

Shri Chouhan said that Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi had pledged from the ramparts of the Red Fort, during his third term, to work with three times the speed and strength. The agriculture and rural development machinery would put its full capabilities behind fulfilling this commitment, he said. Expressing confidence in the progress of the participating districts, Chouhan said competition would intensify ahead of the next review meeting, with several more districts expected to earn recognition for their outstanding work.

Districts Showcase Ground-Level Innovations and Success Stories

The conference recognised the best-performing districts for their exemplary work. District collectors also presented case studies highlighting innovative approaches to improving agricultural productivity, strengthening resilience and increasing farmers’ incomes.

Gadchiroli, Maharashtra: Through water conservation and drought management, the district transformed drought-affected areas into greener landscapes and achieved new milestones in agricultural production.

Alluri Sitharama Raju, Andhra Pradesh: In a low-rainfall region, the district promoted high-value horticultural crops requiring less water, resulting in a significant increase in farmers’ incomes.

Banka, Bihar: The district presented its Lilawaran Natural Farming Land Revival Model, which seeks to end dependence on chemical fertilisers and establish a new wave of natural farming.

Agricultural innovations undertaken by Kishtwar in Jammu and Kashmir, Korba in Chhattisgarh and Fazilka in Punjab were also widely appreciated.

The national conference was attended by Union Ministers of State for Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare Shri Ram Nath Thakur and Shri Bhagirath Choudhary; Union Minister of State for Rural Development Dr Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani; and Union Minister of State Krishan Pal Gurjar. Officials and representatives from the Ministries of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare, Jal Shakti and Rural Development also participated.

Senior officials present included Agriculture Secretary Atish Chandra; Secretary, Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying, Naresh Pal Gangwar; Secretary, Ministry of Food Processing Industries, Avinash Joshi; Secretary, Department of Land Resources, Dilip Kumar; Rural Development Secretary Rohit Kansal; Water Resources Secretary Archana Verma; and ICAR Director General and Secretary, Department of Agricultural Research and Education (DARE), Dr M. L. Jat. Additional Secretary in the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare Maninder Kaur Dwivedi was also present. Agriculture production commissioners and principal secretaries from various states, district collectors from more than 50 districts, and senior field officials from the Centre and state governments participated in the deliberations.

2322442.title: Pursuing Academic Aspirations with Confidence
2322442.body_html:
Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment
Pursuing Academic Aspirations with Confidence
 Rajsamand Rajasthan’s Dr. Chetana Regar’s Journey through the NFSC Scheme
Posted On: 12 OCT 2026 7:03PM by PIB Delhi

The National Fellowship for Scheduled Caste Students (NFSC) Scheme provides eligible scholars with financial assistance to pursue doctoral studies and work towards their academic goals. For many aspiring researchers, financial constraints can make the pursuit of higher education difficult.

The journey of Dr. Chetana Regar from Rajsamand district of Rajasthan illustrates the role such support can play in making higher education possible.

Dr. Chetana Regar, 32, aspired to pursue advanced studies and build a career in academia. However, the financial burden associated with higher education, along with family pressure, made it challenging to pursue her ambitions. She also recognised that doctoral qualifications and research experience may not always receive adequate recognition in the private sector, creating additional uncertainty about professional opportunities.

Her NFSC fellowship assistance began in November 2020 and included fellowship support, House Rent Allowance (HRA) and contingency assistance. The support helped her continue her Ph.D. studies and eased the financial barriers associated with doctoral education. Dr. Regar has stated that pursuing a Ph.D. would not have been possible for her without the fellowship.

The assistance also contributed to a positive personal change: Dr. Regar reported becoming more confident. This confidence has supported her continued commitment to her academic and professional aspirations.

Dr. Regar is currently preparing for Assistant Professor opportunities. Her journey highlights how fellowship support can help eligible scholars pursue doctoral education, build confidence and work towards careers in teaching and research.

2322429.title: From Seasonal Labour to Self-Reliance
2322429.body_html:
Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment
From Seasonal Labour to Self-Reliance
Lucknow’s Santosh Kumar’s Journey through the NSFDC Term Loan Scheme
Posted On: 12 OCT 2026 6:40PM by PIB Delhi

The National Scheduled Castes Finance and Development Corporation (NSFDC), through its Term Loan Scheme, provides financial assistance to eligible beneficiaries to pursue income-generating activities and work towards economic self-reliance.

For many families dependent on seasonal agricultural work, limited income and a lack of financial resources can make it difficult to establish a stable livelihood.

The journey of Shri Santosh Kumar from Gosainganj Block in Lucknow district of Uttar Pradesh illustrates how such assistance can create opportunities for sustainable self-employment.

Shri Santosh Kumar, 36, and his family previously depended on seasonal agricultural work for their livelihood. With an annual family income of only ₹70,000 to ₹80,000, meeting daily household expenses was challenging. Although he possessed driving skills, financial constraints prevented him from purchasing a vehicle and starting his own self-employment venture.

A significant change came when Shri Santosh Kumar received financial assistance of ₹3 lakh under the NSFDC Term Loan Scheme. With this support, he purchased an auto-rickshaw and started his own business. The assistance enabled him to utilise his driving skills productively and establish a source of regular income, reducing his dependence on seasonal agricultural employment.

Today, Shri Santosh Kumar is successfully operating his auto-rickshaw, and his family’s annual income has increased to approximately ₹2.25 lakh, compared with its earlier earnings of ₹70,000 to ₹80,000. This improvement has strengthened the family’s financial position and contributed to a better standard of living. His journey reflects the positive impact of access to financial assistance in enabling individuals to overcome economic constraints and build a more secure future.

Shri Santosh Kumar’s experience highlights how the NSFDC Term Loan Scheme can support self-employment, promote livelihood opportunities and empower beneficiaries to move towards economic independence. By transforming his driving skills into a sustainable source of income, he has taken a significant step towards self-reliance and a more dignified life for his family.

2322423.title: NHRC, India celebrates its 33rd Foundation Day in New Delhi
2322423.body_html:
National Human Rights Commission
NHRC, India celebrates its 33rd Foundation Day in New Delhi
Addressing the gathering as the Chief Guest, Chief Justice of India, Justice Surya Kant lauds the NHRC’s work over the years. Describes the Commission as a guiding light to those adrift in the darkness
Says, SHRCs have a significant role to play, given their proximity to the ground where human rights violation occurs
Commending NHRC for organising the National Conference on Water as the Elixir of Life, the CJI says, the right to water must be understood not only as a right of the present but as a responsibility towards the future
NHRC Chairperson, Justice V. Ramasubramanian says, given the complex challenges facing the world today, human rights institutions throughout the world need to reinvent themselves to continue to be relevant
Posted On: 12 OCT 2026 6:33PM by PIB Delhi

 The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), India today organised a function and National Conference on the theme ‘Water as the Elixir of Life: Advancing Human Dignity through the Right to Water’ to celebrate its 33rd Foundation Day at Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi. The Commission was set up on 12th October 1993. Addressing the function as the Chief Guest, Chief Justice of India, Justice Surya Kant said that the Constitution of India has made extensive promises to every citizen, including for dignity, equality, liberty and justice. These words in the preamble are among the finest ever written and they must be observed day after day in the field, in the lockup, in the hospital ward and in the village at the end of the road.

Lauding the NHRC’s work over the years, Justice Kant said that people sometimes say that “the Commission can only recommend and cannot command, but I would offer an alternative perspective. Picture, for a moment, a solitary lighthouse standing steadfast at the edge of society’s vast, restless sea. Its purpose is not to steal the waves of injustice but to cast a guiding light for those adrift in the darkness.” He said that Human Rights Commissions must investigate complaints, identify systemic failures and ensure that concerns which may otherwise remain invisible receive institutional attention. Civil society can bring ground realities to the forefront while international institutions can contribute scientific knowledge, experience and cooperation.

Justice Surya Kant said that the true measure of a human rights institution is therefore not only the number of cases it decides but whether it can be heard by those who are least able to make themselves heard. This is where the Human Rights Commissions, particularly the State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs), have a significant role to play. In a country as large and diverse as India, the experience of rights is often determined not in the capital, but in a remote village, a particular neighbourhood or even the household. The National Commission can set standards and draw attention to larger patterns, but State Commissions are often closer to the ground where violations occur. They can hear a complaint in the language in which it is made, reach the place where it has occurred and understand the local circumstances in which it has taken place. That proximity gives them not merely an administrative advantage, but a life-altering responsibility.

He also commended the Commission for pairing the celebration with the National Conference on ‘Water as the Elixir of Life.’ He said that the right to water must therefore be understood not only as a right of the present but also as a responsibility towards the future.

Justice Kant said that India itself has made astronomical efforts to expand access to drinking water, including through the provisions of household tap connections in rural areas. That progress deserves commendation, but the next question must be a more demanding one. Is the water safe, reliable and available when the family needs it? Therefore, “the Government must build and maintain the systems through which water reaches people. Courts must intervene when constitutional rights are violated.”

He also appreciated the Commission for the launch of the NHRC, India mobile application and the move towards digitisation of its records. He said that this App make the Commission more accessible to those who have traditionally found it difficult to approach formal institutions.

Before this, thanking the CJI for accepting the invitation to be the Chief Guest for the Foundation Day, NHRC Chairperson, Justice V. Ramasubramanian said that “the office of the CJI has become the single most important, the most powerful, the most vibrant, at the same time, the most vulnerable office of the country which is put to the test of fire (Agni Pariksha), every day, nay, every minute, not necessarily by sacred souls at all times.”

The Chairperson said that “there can be no disagreement on the fact that the world today is a much better place to live than it was hundred years ago. But at the same time, the challenges that we face today are more complex than ever. Therefore, it is the necessity of time that human rights institutions throughout the world reinvent themselves to continue to be relevant.”

Justice Ramasubramanian said that the poorest half of the world’s population is responsible for only 14% of global CO₂ emissions. The world’s richest 10% are responsible for half of all emissions. It is no coincidence that climate and wealth are so closely linked, as they essentially share a common origin: fossil capitalism. Fossil fuels are the source of humanity’s extraordinary progress over the past two centuries but also the source of the extraordinary problems facing us today.

He said that until a few decades ago, our approach to human rights issues was normally two- dimensional. We presumed that it was citizen versus State. But it is not so anymore. Non-State actors now play a huge role, especially after the digital revolution has happened. Today, in the digital world, our opinions can be manipulated, our thought processes can be influenced and our activities, both physical and mental, can be monitored. Therefore, it is time for us, especially when we celebrate NHRC Foundation Day, to take a pledge to reinvent ourselves to face new challenges, reaffirm our commitment to the cause of promotion and protection of human rights and re-engineer our personalities to improve our delivery system.

Earlier, NHRC Member, Justice (Dr.) Bidyut Ranjan Sarangi said that the Commission is committed to promoting and protecting human rights of all including the right to dignity and equality in accordance with the law and the Constitution. In the 33 years of NHRC, there may have been some ups and downs, but it remains committed to its responsibility to serve the cause of human rights. It has expanded its outreach to the doorsteps of the victims of human rights violations through its open hearing and camp sittings.

NHRC Member, Smt. Vijaya Bharathi Sayani said that the concept of human rights is deeply rooted in ancient Indian civilisation, which is also reflected in the Constitution of the country. Quoting Rigvedas and Upanishads, she highlighted that India’s ancient scriptures guided us on how to live together with mutual respect and protect human dignity and wellbeing of all through dialogue and collective strength. Therefore, she said that we must take pride in our heritage and work as equal stakeholders for the protection of eights of girls, children and women, among other vulnerable groups.

In his opening remarks, NHRC Secretary General, Shri Piyush Goyal gave an overview of various dimensions of the Commission’s work towards promoting and protecting life. He said that the subjects of human rights are evolving with time. Climate change and digital world are throwing new challenges. He said that as part of its 33rd Foundation celebration, the Commission has organised a National Conference on the theme ‘Water as the Elixir of Life: Advancing Human Dignity through the Right to Water.’ The two technical sessions include ‘Protection and Restoration of Water Bodies: Safeguarding the Foundation of the Right to Water’ and ‘Protecting Drinking Water Sources: Ensuring Safe and Sustainable Access to Water for All.’ He expressed the hope that the deliberations would result in meaningful recommendations.

Former NHRC Members, Secretary General, Chairpersons and Members of State Human Rights Commissions and other Commissions, members of the judiciary, the diplomatic community, international organisations and civil society, Special Monitors and Special Rapporteurs, senior government officers, academia, human rights defenders, researchers and NHRC senior officers, among others, attended the function.

2322416.title: Union Environment Minister Inaugurates New Office Premises of International Big Cat Alliance
2322416.ministry: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
2322416.body_html:
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
Union Environment Minister Inaugurates New Office Premises of International Big Cat Alliance
55 Lodhi Estate in New Delhi becomes the New Address of the IBCA Headquarters
Posted On: 12 OCT 2026 6:29PM by PIB Delhi

The new office premises of International Big Cat Alliance (IBCA) was inaugurated by the Union Minister of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Shri Bhupender Yadav, at 55 Lodhi Estate, in New Delhi today. DG (IBCA), Dr. S.P. Yadav welcomed the Minister and other dignitaries in the inaugural ceremony and gave a brief overview of IBCA, its activities and programmes. The inaugural ceremony was attended by dignitaries including DG (Forest) and Special Secretary (MoEFCC), Shri Santosh Tewari, and other senior officers from the Ministry.

The event also witnessed participation from the Union Minister of External Affairs; DG, Global Biofuels Alliance (GBA); DG, Coalition for Disaster Resilience Infrastructure (CDRI); DG, International Solar Alliance (ISA); and Heads/Representatives of various international/UN organisations in India, i.e. UN, UNDP, World Bank, UNICEF, ADB, WWF, IUCN, UNEP, FAO and UNDSS, inter alia.

About IBCA

The International Big Cat Alliance, a treaty based inter-governmental international organisation, has been established with headquarters in India, for conservation of seven big cats in the world viz, Lion, Tiger, Leopard, Snow-Leopard, Cheetah, Jaguar and Puma.

The Government of India has pledged an initial contribution of Rs.150 crore for five years (2023-24 to 2027-28). As of now, 29 countries from across the globe, including India, have joined IBCA as members and 5 countries have opted to be Observers and 11 other countries have consented to become members of the Alliance.

During a short span span of two and half years of the establishment of IBCA, following are its important milestones:

  • Two Capacity building programmes organised under the ITEC programme sponsored by MEA, for the foreign participants from different countries.
  • PRIME cat health programme organised for veterinary doctors from 20 countries.
  • Extensive and meaningful participation achieved in International fora such as CITES COP, UNFCCC COP, CITES Standing Committee Meeting etc.
  • Awareness and Outreach activities such as International webinars, Global Photography Competitions held.

2322414.title: From Addiction to Independence
2322414.body_html:
Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment
From Addiction to Independence
Gorakhpur UP’s Imran Khan’s Journey Towards a Drug-Free Life
Posted On: 12 OCT 2026 6:26PM by PIB Delhi

Timely access to medical treatment, counselling and rehabilitation can help individuals recover and rebuild their lives. Substance dependence can affect an individual’s health, family relationships and livelihood.

The journey of Imran Khan (name changed), a 33-year-old self-employed AC mechanic from Gorakhpur district of Uttar Pradesh, illustrates the role of rehabilitation support in helping a person move towards recovery and financial independence.

Imran’s struggle with addiction began at the age of 12, when he started smoking cigarettes under peer pressure. Over time, his dependence expanded to tobacco, gutkha, alcohol, smack, injectable drugs and cannabis. His physical and mental well-being deteriorated, and he experienced behavioural difficulties and financial dependence. His substance dependence affected several aspects of his life, including his relationships, livelihood and social standing.

Imran belonged to a financially disadvantaged family with two brothers and six sisters. His addiction placed emotional and financial strain on the household, while social stigma and strained relationships added to the family’s difficulties. Although he had learned AC repair and other mechanical work, much of his income was spent on substances, preventing him from achieving financial stability. His family remained deeply concerned about his health, and his father experienced heart complications that required bypass surgery. Despite these hardships, his family continued to support him and encouraged him to seek treatment.

On 22 October 2019, Imran received support at Punarjanm Integrated Rehabilitation Centre for Addicts (IRCA), Sonbarasa, Gorakhpur, operated by Basudev Tiwari Sewa Sansthan. He received medical treatment and detoxification support, psychological counselling, motivational therapy and structured rehabilitation. The centre also provided medicines, safe accommodation, nutritious food, emotional support, family counselling and regular monitoring, along with relapse-prevention guidance and livelihood support.

With professional care, continued encouragement and family involvement, Imran developed greater confidence and self-control. He completed a three-month rehabilitation programme and overcame his substance dependence. The intervention helped him focus on his recovery, restore family relationships and return to productive work.

Today, Imran leads a drug-free life and works independently as an AC mechanic, undertaking other mechanical jobs as well. He earns approximately ₹30,000–₹40,000 per month and contributes to household expenses, improving his family’s financial position. His recovery has also helped him regain his family’s trust and respect within society.

Imran’s experience highlights the importance of accessible treatment, psychological support, structured rehabilitation and family involvement in supporting recovery and social reintegration. The assistance provided through Punarjanm IRCA has helped him rebuild his livelihood and move towards a more stable and independent future.

2322389.title: Commerce and Industry Minister Shri Piyush Goyal Calls for Doubling India-UK Bilateral Trade by 2030
2322389.body_html:
Ministry of Commerce & Industry
Commerce and Industry Minister Shri Piyush Goyal Calls for Doubling India-UK Bilateral Trade by 2030
Shri Goyal Highlights Complementary Strengths of India and UK, Calls for Diversifying Trade and Exploring New Export Opportunities
Shri Goyal Identifies Five Key Areas for India-UK Cooperation, Including Clean Energy and Advanced Manufacturing
Rt Hon Jonathan Reynolds MP, Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, UK, Stresses Effective Implementation of CETA to Boost India-UK Trade
Union Minister of State Shri Jitin Prasada Highlights Technology Collaboration as Next Frontier of India-UK Economic Relations
Posted On: 12 OCT 2026 6:04PM by PIB Delhi

Union Minister for Commerce and Industry Shri Piyush Goyal has called upon businesses in India and the United Kingdom to translate the opportunities created by the India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) into expanded trade, investment, partnerships and job creation. Addressing the JETCO Business Plenary under the 16th Session of the India-UK Joint Economic and Trade Committee (JETCO), he said the two countries should aim to double bilateral trade by 2030 and make the India-UK Vision 2035 a framework for greater economic ambition and cooperation.

Shri Goyal said CETA marks a major milestone in the economic partnership between the two countries, providing zero-duty access in the United Kingdom market for most Indian exports while opening up significant opportunities for UK exporters across sectors. The agreement has also opened up new opportunities in services. He added that the Social Security Double Contribution Convention could further benefit both economies through the supply of services at competitive prices and improved profitability.

Emphasising the need to convert the agreement into tangible business outcomes, the Minister said, “This agreement opens the doors businesses have to walk through.” He called for businesses to make the most of the opportunities available under CETA and said that 2030 should not merely mark the end of the decade but the beginning of much greater ambition between the two countries. Referring to the approximately 1,500 days remaining until the end of 2030, he urged businesses to work towards achieving the shared ambition of doubling bilateral trade.

Continuing his address Shri Goyal said India and the UK were complementary economies with considerable potential to expand existing trade, develop new export opportunities and diversify the range of products exchanged. India brings scale, a deepening manufacturing base, world-class digital public infrastructure and the youngest talent pool available anywhere in the world, while the UK brings strengths in research, design, advanced technologies and one of the world's leading financial centres.

Highlighting the existing trade complementarities, the Minister noted that India was a major exporter of smartphones, pharmaceutical products, jewellery, textiles, leather goods, rice and certain agricultural products, iron and non-alloy steel, machinery parts and auto components. On the UK side, he identified potential in the supply of products across the petroleum value chain, technology products in electronics and electrical equipment, medicaments, motor cars and Scotch whisky. He said the wide-ranging CETA had opened up numerous opportunities to expand trade, encourage new exporters and introduce new product lines.

The Minister also highlighted the significant potential for investments in both directions. He noted that several Indian companies had invested substantially in core sectors in the UK, while prominent UK companies had invested in India. He said the Ministry of Commerce and Industry would be willing to cooperate in expanding existing frameworks, enhancing mutual recognition in different areas and supporting both economies to move forward at a faster pace.

Setting out five priority areas for India-UK cooperation, Shri Goyal said infrastructure and clean energy offered opportunities in project development, renewable energy, transmission lines and utility financing to support sustainable growth in both countries.

The second area was advanced manufacturing and resilient supply chains, particularly in electric vehicles, batteries, electronics and precision engineering. He said cooperation should help build competitive manufacturing ecosystems, strengthen supply-chain resilience and enhance confidence between the two trusted partners.

The third priority was technology and innovation. He called for stronger links between educational and research institutions, technology companies and start-ups, alongside greater research and development cooperation. He highlighted opportunities for collaboration in semiconductors, quantum computing and artificial intelligence.

The fourth area was financial services, where he called for greater collaboration between the City of London and GIFT City in Gandhinagar, Gujarat. He identified fintech, insurance, cross-border payments, transition finance and trade finance as areas for cooperation, adding that the two financial centres should work towards becoming a connected pathway to greater progress and prosperity.

The fifth area was healthcare and consumer sectors. Shri Goyal highlighted opportunities in generic pharmaceuticals on the Indian side and branded and innovative pharmaceutical products on the UK side, as well as diagnostics, food processing and consumer goods. He said India's affordability and Britain's strengths in discovery could together become a force multiplier. He added that skills and training across all five areas would be important in expanding business potential, as capital could move quickly across borders but capabilities took time to develop. He stressed the need to invest in mutual understanding and capacity-building to expand trade between the two countries.

Calling for practical support to help businesses benefit from CETA, Shri Goyal emphasised the need to make tariff schedules, rules of origin and documentation requirements accessible through clear instructions. He called for supporting material in plain language and, in the Indian context, regional languages, so that businesses of different sizes and from different regions could navigate the agreement effectively. Referring to a unit in Tirupur in southern India and an engineering firm in the Midlands, he said accessible guidance, including in Tamil where relevant, would help businesses make use of the agreement.

The Minister said one measure of success would be the number of new exporters entering the UK market with new products. He called for greater engagement between businesses on both sides through regular sectoral round tables, sectoral delegations and participation in exhibitions at scale, including as partner countries, to demonstrate the commitment of both countries to implementing the free trade agreement.

Concluding his address, Shri Goyal called for translating the promise of India-UK Vision 2035 into progress on the ground, guided by the principle that when nations grow together, their people prosper together.

Addressing the session Rt Hon Jonathan Reynolds MP, Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade of the United Kingdom, said that the conclusion of the India–UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) marked the beginning of a sustained and practical dialogue between governments and businesses on both sides. He noted that the government-to-government JETCO meeting had concluded ahead of the business dialogue, with the launch of committees and working groups and a joint review of utilisation to address business feedback, resolve implementation issues and improve delivery. With CETA having been in force for almost 100 days, he said there were encouraging signs of businesses in both countries beginning to use the agreement and explore new opportunities across advanced manufacturing, clean energy, life sciences, technology, services and creative industries. He emphasised that the agreement’s success would depend on businesses using it to expand exports, investment and partnerships.

Mr. Reynolds stressed the need for practical support to help businesses, particularly MSMEs and first-time exporters, understand tariff reductions, rules of origin, customs procedures, regulatory requirements and procurement opportunities. He underlined the importance of frank and constructive feedback from businesses to identify implementation challenges and areas where further government action could facilitate trade and investment. He said that business feedback would be taken up through CETA’s utilisation review, committees and working groups, adding that the agreement was a starting point for further expansion of India–UK trade relations. He called for translating the commitment to trade and cooperation into tangible outcomes, including contracts, investments, commercialisation of technologies and job creation in both countries, and reaffirmed the importance of keeping businesses at the centre of implementation.

Union Minister of State for Commerce and Industry Shri Jitin Prasada in his address said that sustained engagement between India and the UK business communities through business missions and exchanges between industrial associations would help companies identify prospective partners, explore opportunities and strengthen commercial ties across regions and enterprises of different sizes. He highlighted technological collaboration as the next frontier of India–UK economic relations, particularly in artificial intelligence, semiconductors and data centres. He noted that the UK’s strengths in research and development, combined with India’s engineering talent, digital market and ability to deploy technologies at scale, offered opportunities for collaboration. Referring to the Technology Security Initiative agreed in 2024, he said both countries could work towards developing trusted and affordable technologies for global markets. He emphasised that continued government–industry engagement would strengthen business confidence and called for measuring progress at the next JETCO through partnerships signed, factories opened and jobs created.

This was the first JETCO session following the signing and entry into force of the India–UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) on 15 July 2026. The Ministers reviewed early business uptake of CETA, bilateral trade and investment developments, and priorities for the year ahead.
The JETCO coincided with the visit of seven mayors and a combined authority leader from the North of England. It supported a broader programme of engagement involving government, business, universities, innovators and regional leaders from both countries, including parallel visits by the UK's Secretaries of State for Scotland and for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs.
Both sides undertook a Joint Utilisation Review of CETA and welcomed the speed with which businesses in both countries have used the agreement. The Ministers also welcomed the establishment of sub-committees and working groups under CETA and exchange of contact points for these sub-committees and working groups. The Ministers agreed that the committees will engage and develop a practical forward roadmap identifying the priority areas and issues on which they will work.

The UK India Business Council (UKIBC), the strategic and knowledge partner to the Great North delegation, is supporting a first-of-its-kind mayoral mission to India bringing together leaders from five Combined Authorities across the North of England.

UKIBC has provided the delegation with strategic and market insights on India, identified bilateral opportunities across priority sectors, and facilitated engagement with Indian industry and government. The mission forms part of UKIBC's wider work with Northern regions, which includes identifying each region's strongest proposition in India, developing market strategies and engagement plans, and building long-term partnerships with Indian businesses and institutions. These efforts aim to translate intent into practical programmes on the ground.

2322388.title: “Indian Telecom Services Performance Indicator Report” for the Quarter April - June, 2026
2322388.body_html:
Ministry of Communications
“Indian Telecom Services Performance Indicator Report” for the Quarter April - June, 2026
Posted On: 12 OCT 2026 6:00PM by PIB Delhi

TRAI today has released the “Indian Telecom Services Performance Indicator Report” for the quarter ending 30th June 2026. This Report provides a broad perspective of the Telecom Services in India and presents the key parameters and growth trends of the Telecom Services as well as Cable TV, DTH & Radio Broadcasting services in India for the period covering 1st April 2026 to 30th June 2026 compiled mainly on the basis of information furnished by the Service Providers.

Executive Summary of the Report is enclosed. The complete Report is available on TRAI’s website (www.trai.gov.in and under the link http://www.trai.gov.in/release-publication/reports/performance-indicators-reports). For any suggestion or any clarification pertaining to this report, Shri Vijay Kumar, Advisor (F&EA), TRAI may be contacted on Tel. +91-20907773 and e-mail:     fea1-div@trai.gov.in.

The Indian Telecom Services Performance Indicators

April–June 2026

Executive Summary

  1. Total number of Internet subscribers increased from 1092.79 million at the end of March 2026 to 1114.17 million at the end of June 2026, registering a quarterly rate of growth of 96%. Out of 1114.17 million Internet subscribers, number of Wired Internet subscribers are 47.73 million and number of Wireless Internet subscribers are 1066.43 million.

Composition of Internet Subscription

  1. The Internet subscriber base is comprised of Broadband Internet subscriber base of 1087.50 million and Narrowband Internet subscriber base of 26.67 million.
  2. The broadband Internet subscriber base increased by 2.03% from 1065.88 million at the end of March 2026 to 1087.50 million at the end of June 2026. The narrowband Internet subscriber base decreased by 0.89% from 26.91 million at the end of March 2026 to 26.67 million at the end of June 2026.
  3. Wireline subscribers decreased from 48.25 million at the end of March 2026 to 47.82 million at the end of June 2026 with a quarterly rate of decline 0.88%. On Y-O-Y basis, wireline subscriptions increased by 0.71% at the end of quarter ending June 2026.
  4. Wireline Tele-density decreased from 3.38% at the end of March 2026 to 3.35% at the end of June 2026 with quarterly rate of decline 1.06%.
  5. Monthly Average Revenue per User (ARPU)  for wireless service increased by 1.19%, from ₹184.91 in quarter ending March 2026 to ₹187.12 in quarter ending June 2026. On Y-O-Y basis, monthly ARPU for wireless service increased by 3.11% in this quarter.
  6. The ARPU per month for the pre-paid segment is ₹200.72 and the ARPU per month for the post-paid segment is ₹114.26 for quarter ending June 2026.                              
  7. On an all-India average, the overall MOU per month decreased by 2.65% from 959 in quarter ending March 2026 to 933 in quarter ending June 2026. 
  8. Prepaid MOU per subscriber is 1055 and Postpaid MOU per subscriber per month is 279 in quarter ending June 2026.
  9. Average revenue realization per GB for wireless data usage decreased from ₹7.51 in quarter ending March 2026 to ₹7.13 in quarter ending June 2026 with quarterly rate of decline of 5.07%.
  10. Number of wireless (Mobile) data subscribers has increased from 1026.75 million at the end of March 2026 to 1045.55 million at the end of June 2026 with quarterly rate of growth of 1.86%.  Further, total volume of wireless (mobile) data usage also increased from 77,953 PB during quarter ending March 2026 to 84,424 PB during quarter ending June 2026 with growth of 8.30%.
  11. Average Wireless (Mobile) Data Usage per wireless data subscriber per month increased from 26.70 GB during quarter ending March 2026 to 28.39 GB during June 2026 with quarterly rate of growth 6.32%.
  12. Gross Revenue (GR), Applicable Gross Revenue (ApGR) and Adjusted Gross Revenue (AGR) of Telecom Service Sector for the quarter ending June 2026 has been ₹1,06,797 Crore, ₹101,036 crore and ₹88,796 Crore respectively.  GR increased by 1.60%, ApGR by 2.43% and AGR increased by 2.40% in the quarter ending June 2025, as compared to previous quarter. 
  13. The Y-O-Y rate of growth in GR, ApGR and AGR in the quarter ending June 2026 over the same quarter in last year have been 10.50%, 9.52% and 9.19% respectively.
  14. Pass Through Charges decreased from ₹12,494 Crore in the quarter ending March 2026 to ₹12,241 Crore in the quarter ending June 2026 with quarterly rate of decline of 2.02%. The Y-O-Y rate of growth 17.06% has been recorded in pass-through charges in the quarter ending June 2026.
  15. The License Fee increased from ₹6,936 Crore in the quarter ending March 2026 to ₹7,103 Crore in the quarter ending June 2026. The quarterly and the Y-O-Y rates of growth in license fees are 2.41% and 9.18% respectively in this quarter. 

Service-wise composition of Adjusted Gross Revenue

  1. Access services contributed 83.85% of the total Adjusted Gross Revenue of telecom services. In Access services, Gross Revenue (GR), Applicable Gross Revenue (ApGR), Adjusted Gross Revenue (AGR), License Fee, Spectrum Usage Charges (SUC) and Pass Through Charges increased by 1.43%, 2.86%, 2.72%, 2.73%, 2.83% and -8.83% respectively in the quarter ending June 2026.
  2. The number of total telephone subscribers in India increased from 1,330.58 million at the end of March 2026 to 1,348.08 million at the end of June 2026, registering a rate of growth 1.31% over the previous quarter. This reflects Year-On-Year (Y-O-Y) rate of growth of 10.65% over the same quarter of last year. The overall Tele-density in India increased from 93.26% in the quarter ending March 2026 to 94.31% in the quarter ending June 2026.

Trends in Telephone subscribers and Tele-density in India

 

  1. Telephone subscribers in Urban areas increased from 778.79 million at the end of March 2026 to 792.06 million at the end of June 2026 and Urban Tele-density also increased from 151.47% to 153.43% during the same period.
  2. Rural telephone numbers reached 551.79 million at the end of March 2026 to 556.01 million at the end of June 2026 and Rural Tele-density also increased from 60.46% to 60.89% during the same period.

 

  1. Out of the total subscription, the share of Rural subscription decreased from 41.47% at the end of March 2026 to 41.24% at the end of June 2026.

 

Composition of Telephone Subscribers

   

  1. With a net addition of 17.92 million subscribers during the quarter, the total wireless (mobile+FWA) subscriber base increased from 1282.33 million at the end of March 2026 to 1300.25 million at the end of June 2026, registering a rate of growth 1.40% over the previous quarter. On     Y-O-Y basis, wireless subscriptions increased at the rate of 11.05% during the year. 
  2. Wireless (mobile + FWA) Tele-density increased from 89.88% at the end of March 2026 to 90.96% at the end of June 2026 with quarterly rate of growth 1.21%.
  3. With a net addition of 16.66 million subscribers during the quarter, the wireless (mobile) subscriber base increased from 1265.73 million at the end of March 2026 to 1282.38 million at the end of June 2026, registering a rate of growth 1.32% over the previous quarter. On Y-O-Y basis, wireless subscriptions also increased at the rate of 10.26% during the year. 
  4. Wireless (mobile) Tele-density increased from 88.71% at the end of March 2026 to 89.71% at the end of June 2026 with quarterly rate of growth of 1.13%.

2322060.title: Central Bureau of Narcotics (CBN) M.P. Unit seizes over 4.2 tonnes of poppy straw in two operations; Three persons arrested
2322060.body_html:
Ministry of Finance
Central Bureau of Narcotics (CBN) M.P. Unit seizes over 4.2 tonnes of poppy straw in two operations; Three persons arrested
Posted On: 11 OCT 2026 10:48PM by PIB Delhi

In continuation of its sustained anti-drug drive, the Central Bureau of Narcotics (CBN), Madhya Pradesh Unit, conducted two successful operations during the past week resulting in the seizure of 4,209.80 kg poppy straw, two vehicles and 100 bags of wheat used as cover cargo. Three persons have been arrested in the two cases under the relevant provisions of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985.

 

SEIZURE AT A GLANCE

  • Total poppy straw seized: 4,209.80 kg
  • Vehicles seized: 02 (one Tata truck and one container truck)
  • Wheat bags seized as cover cargo: 100
  • Total persons arrested: 03

 

On 05.10.2026, acting on specific intelligence, officers of CBN Neemuch intercepted a container truck bearing Haryana registration on the Udaipur–Chittorgarh highway. A search of the vehicle resulted in the recovery of 929.08 kg poppy straw, comprising lanced poppy straw, unlanced poppy straw (UPS) and poppy straw powder, concealed beneath 39 plastic sacks of various colours. The vehicle and contraband were seized, and one person was arrested under the relevant provisions of the NDPS Act, 1985.

 

Contraband seized along with container truck

Acting on specific intelligence, officers of CBN intercepted a Tata truck bearing Rajasthan registration on the Gandhisagar–Bhanpura road, in Mandsaur, Madhya Pradesh, on 09.10.2026. A thorough search at the CBN office, Garoth, led to the recovery of 3,280.72 kg poppy straw concealed beneath 100 bags of wheat being transported as cover cargo. The poppy straw, truck and wheat bags were seized, and both occupants were arrested under the relevant provisions of the NDPS Act, 1985.


Contraband seized along with Tata Truck

 

Further investigation in both cases is underway to identify the source of the contraband, intended recipients and other persons involved in the trafficking networks.

The Central Bureau of Narcotics (CBN) remains firmly committed to the vision of “Safe Use and Prevent Abuse of Drugs or Medicines” and “Nasha Mukt Bharat” and continues to undertake intelligence-driven enforcement and preventive awareness initiatives against the illegal trafficking, diversion and abuse of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances.

2322059.title: DRI seizes around 5.8 kg foreign-origin gold worth Rs. 9 crores from a secret cavity in car, uncovering a sophisticated gold smuggling modus operandi; two arrested
2322059.body_html:
Ministry of Finance
DRI seizes around 5.8 kg foreign-origin gold worth Rs. 9 crores from a secret cavity in car, uncovering a sophisticated gold smuggling modus operandi; two arrested
Posted On: 11 OCT 2026 10:46PM by PIB Delhi

Continuing its sustained crackdown on organised gold smuggling, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI), in an intelligence led operation, intercepted a car carrying two passengers travelling from Kolkata to Hyderabad at Visakhapatnam during 08–09 October 2026. The interception followed a prolonged chase by officers, who maintained heightened vigilance along the National Highway.

Seized 5.8 kg gold

A thorough search of the vehicle, involving prolonged examination and systematic rummaging, led to the detection of a specially fabricated concealed cavity beneath the leg space of the front co-passenger seat. Three packets containing 5,832.90 grams of foreign-origin gold of 24-carat, valued at approximately Rs. 8.98 crore, were recovered from the cavity. The occupants admitted that the gold had been smuggled into India through the Indo-Bangladesh border and was being transported to Hyderabad.

The recovered gold was seized under the relevant provisions of the Customs Act, 1962. Both occupants were arrested.

The case bears a striking resemblance to another major recent seizure by DRI on 18-19 September 2026, when officers intercepted two Thar vehicles near Palwal Toll Plaza near- Delhi and recovered more than 15 kg of foreign-origin gold valued at more than Rs.23 crore from sophisticated concealed cavities fabricated in the vehicles’ chassis. Preliminary intelligence in that case indicated that the gold had been smuggled from Myanmar.

These cases highlight the increasingly sophisticated methods employed by organised gold-smuggling networks to transport contraband across the country by concealing it in specially engineered cavities in vehicles. DRI remains resolute in identifying such evolving concealment techniques, dismantling smuggling networks and safeguarding the country’s economic and revenue interests.

****

Union Minister for Communications and Development of North Eastern Region Jyotiraditya M. Scindia, will undertake a series of important engagements in Mizoram on October 12 and 13, 2026. This will be Scindia’s second visit to the state as DoNER minister.  His two day long engagements reflect Government of India’s continued commitment to the development of the Northeast, youth empowerment and deeper engagement with the region’s stakeholders.

During his visit, Minister Scindia will participate in development-related programmes, interact with students and civil society representatives, and engage with the banking sector at the North East Bankers’ Conclave 3.0.

12 October 2026 ---

Shri Scindia will arrive in Aizawl and travel to Tuivamit, where he will inaugurate projects and lay foundation stones, marking an important step towards strengthening development initiatives in Mizoram.

He will subsequently visit Mizoram University for an interaction with students, providing an opportunity to engage with the youth of the University and students of MDoNER’s Ashtalakshmi Darshan Program.

On the second day of his visit, Shri Scindia will return to Mizoram University to inaugurate and deliver the keynote address at the North East Bankers’ Conclave 3.0. The conclave will bring the banking sector into focus as a key partner in advancing financial inclusion, improving access to credit and supporting economic growth across the Northeastern region.

2322003.title: Prime Minister  Shri Narendra Modi participates in golden jubilee celebrations of Jaigopal Garodia Hindu Vidyalaya Matriculation Higher Secondary School, Chennai, Tamil Nadu
2322003.body_html:
Prime Minister's Office
Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi participates in golden jubilee celebrations of Jaigopal Garodia Hindu Vidyalaya Matriculation Higher Secondary School, Chennai, Tamil Nadu
The energy of our youth inspires great faith in India's future: PM
Today's youth aspires to be the strength driving the vision of a 'Viksit Bharat'; the innovative ideas and solutions needed for a Viksit Bharat, will shape the future of not just India, but the entire globe: PM
Given the infinite opportunities available in India today, I want every young person to see their future on that massive canvas; Because, this is your time, This is your opportunity: PM
I also recall the great saint Thiruvalluvar ji, whose teachings are crucial for all students; recently, I had the opportunity to present a Russian translation of the Tirukkural to Russian President Putin: PM
The Tirukkural is a wonderful guide for all those who wish to keep learning something new throughout their lives: PM
In one of his very famous Kurals, Thiruvalluvar ji teaches us that along with learning something, it is also necessary to adopt it in one's life: PM
While India prepares to host the 2030 Commonwealth Games, we are also moving forward with the dream of hosting the 2036 Olympics: PM
Posted On: 11 OCT 2026 7:05PM by PIB Delhi

Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi today participated in the golden jubilee celebrations of Jaigopal Garodia Hindu Vidyalaya Matriculation Higher Secondary School in Chennai, Tamil Nadu. Highlighting the profound spiritual significance of the day, the Prime Minister expressed his immense joy at visiting the holy land of Shiva and Shakti on the very first day of Navratri. He stated that experiencing the positive energy, excitement, and vibrant enthusiasm of the youth while meeting the devotees of Mother Saraswati made for an incredibly auspicious start to the festival."I can see the future of India in the eyes of all of you,” noted Shri Modi.

Recognizing the immense potential of the younger generation, the Prime Minister emphasized that today's youth possess a strong desire to become the driving force behind the vision of a 'Viksit Bharat’.  He stated that the new ideas and solutions required to achieve this national goal will ultimately shape not only the country's destiny but the future of the entire globe."Today, the world is looking for solutions, and you have the potential to provide those solutions,” asserted Shri Modi.

Encouraging the students to dream on a massive scale, the Prime Minister urged every youth to envision their future upon the vast canvas of infinite opportunities currently emerging across the nation. He expressed absolute confidence that this collective national dream is entirely within their grasp during this era of unprecedented possibility."Together, We Will Do It!” affirmed Shri Modi.

Recounting a deeply personal anecdote, the Prime Minister revealed the interesting inspiration behind his visit, recalling a meeting with Girija Amma and several children in Nagercoil a few months prior."Her profound dedication, self-confidence, and unwavering devotion towards the future of the country left an unprecedented impression on my mind,” remarked Shri Modi.

Fulfilling the promise made during that initial meeting, the Prime Minister shared that Girija Amma's warm affection and his own deep respect for the historic institution compelled him to accept her invitation to the golden jubilee celebration. "I extend my heartiest congratulations to the Vishwa Hindu Vidya Kendra and the entire Hindu Vidyalaya family for this magnificent journey of Fifty Years,” affirmed Shri Modi.

Tracing the institution's highly inspiring trajectory, the Prime Minister noted that the Vishwa Hindu Vidya Kendra began as a very small school in Chennai's 'West Mambalam' in 1975 with merely seven students and limited resources. He praised the founders for relying on their strong willpower and an unbreakable spirit of service to overcome initial hardships and drive the institution forward despite lacking modern facilities or a permanent building."That is why, despite every difficulty, this institution kept moving forward,” observed Shri Modi.

Highlighting the massive expansion born from those humble beginnings, the Prime Minister celebrated how that small initial effort evolved into a massive educational movement over the decades. He noted the impressive scale of the institution's current reach across the state."Today you have 15 institutions in different parts of Tamil Nadu,” noted Shri Modi.

Honoring the foundational figures of the institution, the Prime Minister respectfully remembered the crucial contributions of Shri Jaigopal Garodia in constructing the school's building. He extended his deep gratitude to all the teachers, staff, parents, and alumni who dedicated their lives to making the Hindu Vidyalaya journey a resounding success."Fifty years of dedication, fifty years of commitment, fifty years of shaping young lives,” remarked Shri Modi.

Praising the institution for successfully blending academic education with strong patriotic values, the Prime Minister recalled mentioning Girija Amma in his 'Mann Ki Baat' program for brilliantly inspiring children to save just one rupee daily for the nation's soldiers. He commended the incredible collective impact of thousands of children joining this resolution to successfully raise forty lakh rupees."Indeed, what an inspiring example!” affirmed Shri Modi.

Emphasizing the profound power of incremental efforts, the Prime Minister stated that small contributions can generate a massive positive impact on society. He praised the Hindu Vidyalaya family for actively cultivating a great legacy of values, whether through supporting the needy during natural disasters or actively participating in cleanliness drives."Even a small effort can create a very big impact,” observed Shri Modi.

Invoking ancient wisdom, the Prime Minister paid homage to the great saint Thiruvalluvar, emphasizing that his teachings hold immense contemporary relevance for today's students. He proudly shared a recent diplomatic interaction where he presented a Russian translation of the Thirukkural to President Putin."His teachings are very important for all of you students,” noted Shri Modi.

Elaborating on the timeless guidance of the Thirukkural, the Prime Minister praised the text as a wonderful compass for lifelong learners. He highlighted a famous Kural by Thiruvalluvar that stresses the absolute necessity of actively applying learned knowledge to one's daily life, calling it a vital lesson for the students."Along with learning something, it is also essential to adopt it in one's life,” affirmed Shri Modi.

Highlighting the deep cultural ties that bind the nation, the Prime Minister noted that the great poet Mahakavi Bharathiyar was profoundly influenced by the spiritual and national consciousness he experienced in Kashi. He encouraged the students to read and draw inspiration from the poet's expansive life and philosophy."The atmosphere of Kashi, filled with spiritual and national consciousness, had a deep impact on his thoughts,” observed Shri Modi.

Connecting his own parliamentary constituency to this shared heritage, the Prime Minister shared that the people of Kashi still fondly remember Mahakavi Bharathiyar today. He urged the youth to actively adopt the poet's famous mantra 'Achamillai, Achamillai' (Fearless, Fearless) to aggressively pursue their ideas and dreams."Dream big, think differently, and be fearless,” asserted Shri Modi.

Reflecting on his own life experiences, the Prime Minister explained that his deep understanding of the country was forged through extensive travel and learning directly from the people across different regions. He fondly recalled his participation in the Ekta Yatra from Kanyakumari to Kashmir in the early 1990s, where his enduring acquaintance with Girija Amma first began."Since then this acquaintance of ours has remained,” remarked Shri Modi.

Expressing his profound personal connection to the state, the Prime Minister stated that his extensive travels allowed him to intimately understand and appreciate the vast diversity of the nation. "The love that exists in my life for the Tamil language and Tamil culture has also been born from these very experiences,” affirmed Shri Modi.

Encouraging the students to actively engage in national integration, the Prime Minister urged the youth to travel widely and proudly carry Tamil culture wherever they go. He advised them to share Tamil poetry, stories, and traditions while actively forging friendships with people from vastly different backgrounds to strengthen the unity of the nation."The unity of our nation is built by the friendships you make,” asserted Shri Modi.

Detailing the unprecedented structural changes transforming the nation's academic landscape, the Prime Minister highlighted the massive expansion of opportunities available to the new generation. He provided stark statistical evidence, noting that the number of universities in the country has surged from 750 in 2014 to over 1,300 today, while colleges have increased from 38,000 to over 52,000, alongside the establishment of numerous new IITs, IIMs, IIITs, and AIIMS."The entire landscape of education in the country is changing today,” noted Shri Modi.

Underscoring the qualitative improvements driven by the new education policy, the Prime Minister celebrated the rapidly growing global recognition of domestic institutions. He pointed out that the number of Indian universities featured in the QS Rankings has dramatically increased from just 14 in 2015 to 52 in the latest rankings, directly resulting in vastly expanded choices for students."More institutions, more choices, and more opportunities for you,” affirmed Shri Modi.

Addressing the diverse aspirations of the youth, the Prime Minister acknowledged that many students wish to pursue non-traditional careers, particularly in sports. He assured them that the country is actively building new sports infrastructure and providing better training and support to ensure sports is treated as a viable profession rather than mere entertainment, which is already raising the nation's stature internationally."Young athletes are getting better training and support,” noted Shri Modi.

Outlining highly ambitious national sporting goals, the Prime Minister announced that the country is aggressively preparing to host the 2030 Commonwealth Games and is advancing with the grand dream of hosting the 2036 Olympics. He declared that with the upcoming influx of massive global sporting events, the youth now possess the ultimate platform, the potential, and the full backing of the state."The opportunities are endless, and I am confident your generation will take India to new heights in the world of sports as well,” asserted Shri Modi.

Expressing his confidence in the younger generation, the Prime Minister stated that engaging with the students and feeling their vibrant dreams had significantly strengthened his belief in a glorious national future. He declared the youth to be the ultimate heroes who will shape and define the coming era."The future of India will be very glorious, and the biggest heroes of that future are you,” affirmed Shri Modi.

Reaffirming his absolute trust in their capabilities, the Prime Minister praised the immense talent, confidence, and capability of the students present. He invited the gathered youth to join him in making some massive, historic national resolutions."Today I want to reiterate some big resolutions with all of you,” remarked Shri Modi.

Concluding his address with a highly interactive and energetic pledge, the Prime Minister led the massive crowd in a resounding chant of "We will Do it!" to commit to a series of grand national goals. He urged the youth to fiercely dedicate themselves to building a Developed India by 2047, becoming a top-three global economy, establishing a self-reliant global manufacturing hub, hosting the Olympics, and placing an Indian on the moon.
